newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO outlines shape of expansion deal with Russia.
newsitem.headline: NATO outlines shape of expansion deal with Russia.

text.p: NATO proposed on Monday that it and Russia should station liaison officers in their respective military commands as the outlines of a possible deal on the Atlantic alliance's eastwards enlargement became clearer.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said the formal proposal was one of many ideas for building a close post-Cold War relationship between the two former foes, possibly enshrined in a charter creating permanent institutions for joint action.

"NATO is working on ways to flesh out the substance of a new, permanent relationship with Russia," Solana wrote in an article published on Monday in the English-language International Herald Tribune newspaper.

Solana also said in several newspaper interviews, timed to coincide with a visit of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed to NATO's headquarters, that enlargement to take in new members from central and eastern Europe would go ahead.
But he stressed such countries would be joining a "new NATO" which posed no threat to Moscow and would be part of a new European security order in which Russia would play a full role.

A stony-faced Lebed entered NATO's headquarters on his first visit to the West carrying what he said were new proposals to end tensions with Moscow over enlargement. He cautioned NATO to move with extreme caution.
"Every step must be calculated. Take stock, take stock and take stock again," he told reporters after a first round of talks, but he appeared to leave open the possibility of a deal.

"I came to say let's work together, let's solve the problem...of modernising, reforming NATO, the establishment of special, as we say, relations between Russia and NATO, expressed in an agreement or treaty with legal status and then, further, take a decision on expansion or non-expansion," he said.
Lebed said his new proposals would be presented later on Monday at a meeting with NATO ambassadors.

Solana and NATO capitals, keen to shift the emphasis of the talks with Lebed to areas of agreement, say the two sides must first build on their ground-breaking cooperation in the current alliance-led peace mission in Bosnia.

"Why not build on this by having Russian officers permanently at NATO Supreme Command Headquarters and, reciprocally, NATO liaison officers at the Russian General Staff?," Solana wrote in the newspaper article.
Alliance officials said Solana would detail the proposals, including the charter idea, in the talks with Lebed, President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser.
He stressed applicant nations had a right to join "the Euro-Atlantic community to which they feel they legitimately belong".

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry proposed at a NATO meeting in Norway late last month that the alliance "throw open its doors" to Russia to help convince its old enemy its intentions were not hostile.
Moscow opposes NATO's plans to take in new members from former communist Europe, particularly its former Warsaw Pact allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Western nations now say a limited expansion of the alliance is certain to begin next year but hope they can win Russian acquiescence by offering Moscow an upgraded relationship taking account of its weight in world affairs.
Perry's plan, creating standing arrangements for consultation and joint action between Russia and the alliance, would stop just short of full membership for Russia itself.
